**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

- Answer FOUR Questions.
- TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.
- Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

SECTION A: question 1 is compulsory in the sense that the candidate answers either 1A* or 1B* (the two Starred questions) and one other question from the section (2, 3 or 4). SECTION B: answer ONE question (5, 6 or 7). SECTION C: answer ONE question (8, 9 or 10).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A* or 1B* and one other Question from this section.

**1. Either**

**A\* (Starred question)** Study the following extracts on the origin, evolution and collapse of German colonial rule in Cameroon and then answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets).

**EXTRACT I**

> "...In many ways Nachtigal was the personal envoy of the two Great German Commercial Houses operating along the Cameroon coast, since he was instructed...to claim for Germany whatever land the agents of the two German firms had acquired already or would acquire...
> Two documents were signed at the time. The **first** was an expression of the wishes of the local chiefs... [Any contrary action to] this document was important as far as later developments were concerned. The second document was the [line 5] treaty between the Germans and the kings. Sovereignty over the land was given to the German traders under certain conditions..."

**EXTRACT II**

> "When local Douala kings agreed to hand over their sovereignty to the Germans...the Cameroon...coastal strip...became a German colony. The Baptists at Victoria were replaced...and the capital was [later] established at Buea. Almost immediately, the Germans began to regret their promises to the Douala [line 10] kings...The Germans independently began to explore the interior in order to see for themselves where the...goods were coming from and from this time on hostilities with the ...chiefs became inevitable..."

**EXTRACT III**

> "German rule came to a swift end...when the circumstances of the First World War meant the defeat and expulsion of the Germans from Cameroon. The capitulation of the German garrison...marked the end of the German Kamerun Protectorate. Cameroon was provisionally divided...but boundary adjustments were later made in an agreement signed [line 15] on 10 July 1919."

*Source: T Eyongetah and R Brain; A History of the Cameroon, Essex: Longman, 1974, pages 63 and 65.*

(The "[line n]" marks show the line numbers printed in the margin of the original extracts (lines 5, 10 and 15); the questions refer to them.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Give the **name** of the state official who assigned Nachtigal to carry out the mission described in Extract I.

(ii) Write down the names of the **two** commercial houses mentioned in Extract I.

[1+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The state official.** Otto von Bismarck, the German Chancellor. In 1884 he made Gustav Nachtigal Imperial Commissioner for West Africa and sent him on the gunboat *Möwe* to the coast of Cameroon and Togo to claim for Germany the lands in which German traders were already established. (1 mark)

**(ii) The two commercial houses.**
1. **C. Woermann** (the Hamburg firm of Adolph Woermann);
2. **Jantzen and Thormählen** (also of Hamburg).

Their agents at Douala (Eduard Schmidt for Woermann and Johannes Voss for Jantzen and Thormählen) were the German signatories of the treaty with the Duala kings. (2 marks)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) What **code name** was used to identify what has been described as the **"first document"** in Extract I, *line 4*?

(ii) State **two** conditions accepted by the Germans in the **"second document"** as indicated in Extract I, *line 5*.

(iii) What **two** wishes expressed by the local chiefs in the first document were not respected by the Germans?

[1+2+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The "first document".** It is identified as the **Memorandum** of the Duala chiefs (the "memorandum of wishes" in which Kings Bell and Akwa and the other chiefs listed what they expected from the Germans in return for the treaty). (1 mark)

**(ii) Two conditions accepted by the Germans in the treaty (the "second document", the Germano-Duala Treaty of 12 July 1884).** Any two of:
1. The Duala would keep the **ownership of their land**: their farms, their villages and their burial places (cemeteries) were not to be taken from them.
2. The Duala kings would **keep their middleman position in trade**: trade with the people of the interior would stay in the hands of the Duala.
3. The Germans would **respect the customs and laws** of the Duala and the authority of their chiefs over their own people.
4. The Duala would continue to receive the **customs dues (comey)** that the traders paid to them.
(2 marks: 1 mark for each valid condition)

**(iii) Two wishes of the chiefs that were not respected.** Any two of:
1. **Land.** The Germans later took Duala land for administration buildings, plantations and the European quarter. The most famous case is the expropriation of the Duala from the Joss Plateau area at Douala, planned from about 1910, which led to the protest of Rudolf Duala Manga Bell and his execution in 1914.
2. **Trade with the interior.** The Duala had asked to remain the middlemen, but the Germans soon explored the interior by themselves, opened direct trade routes and put German firms and later the railways in contact with the producers, so that the Duala lost their trading monopoly.
3. **Their rights as rulers and their income.** The chiefs' powers were reduced by German officials and the dues and payments they had expected were cut down.
(2 marks: 1 mark for each valid wish)
themes: european trade on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) In which year and by which religious organizations were the Baptists in Victoria replaced (Extract II)?

(ii) Give the **main reason** why the capital was later established in Buea and the name of the colonial governor under whom the decision was taken.

[2+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Year and organisations.** The English Baptist missionaries (founded at Victoria, now Limbe, by Alfred Saker in 1858) withdrew in **1886**. They were replaced by the German **Basel Mission** (Swiss-German Protestant mission). The German Catholic missionaries, the **Pallottine Fathers**, arrived in 1890 and also took part in the German mission field. (2 marks: 1 for the year, 1 for the Basel Mission or the Pallottines)

**(ii) Reason and governor.**
- **Main reason:** the **climate**. Buea lies on the slopes of Mount Cameroon at about 900 metres, where the air is cool and healthy and much less malarial than the swampy coast of Douala. The Germans wanted a healthy place for their officials. (Also, the area was in the middle of the new plantations.) (1 mark)
- **Governor:** **Jesko von Puttkamer**, who moved the seat of the colonial government to Buea in 1901 (he was Governor from 1895 to 1907). (1 mark)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Give the location of the German garrison and the name of the military officer whose capitulation marked the end of German rule in Kamerun (Extract III).

(ii) In which year did the event cited in (d) (i) take place?

(iii) Write down the **code name** that was given to the boundary adjustments mentioned in Extract III.

[2+1+1 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Location and officer.** The last German garrison was at **Mora**, on the Mora Mountain in the Mandara Mountains of the Far North. It was commanded by **Captain Ernst von Raben**, who surrendered to the Allied (British and French) forces. (2 marks: 1 for the place, 1 for the officer)

**(ii) Year.** **1916** (the capitulation took place in February 1916, after Yaounde had fallen on 1 January 1916). (1 mark)

**(iii) Code name of the boundary adjustments.** The **Milner-Simon Declaration** of 10 July 1919, signed by the British Colonial Secretary Lord Milner and the French Colonial Minister Henri Simon. It fixed the boundary between the British and the French zones, and it confirmed the partition of Cameroon. (1 mark)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) What effects did the defeat and expulsion of the Germans from Cameroon (mentioned in Extract III) have on Cameroon.

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any four of the following effects (1 mark each):

1. **Partition of the territory.** Cameroon was divided between Britain and France: France took the larger part (about four fifths) and Britain a narrow strip along the Nigerian border (British Cameroons, divided into Northern and Southern Cameroons). The partition was confirmed by the Milner-Simon Declaration of 1919 and by the League of Nations Mandates of 1922.
2. **End of German rule and new colonial masters.** Cameroonians passed from German to British and French control, under League of Nations mandates and later UN trusteeships.
3. **Division of peoples and families.** The new frontier cut across ethnic groups and communities, separating kinsmen and splitting some trading areas.
4. **Different colonial systems and languages.** The French part was run through direct rule and assimilation with French as the language; the British part was run through indirect rule (as part of Nigeria) with English. This created the English and French-speaking cultures of Cameroon.
5. **Expulsion of German settlers and missions, and the fate of German property.** German officials, planters and missionaries were expelled, and German plantations and companies were seized, later put up for sale (some were bought back by Germans in the 1920s). The Basel Mission was replaced by other missions.
6. **Economic reorientation.** Trade and plantations were reorganised according to the interests of Britain and France, and the colonial railways and roads were extended to serve their own markets.
7. **Hope of a better life and later demand for reunification.** The divided country became the starting point of the later demand for reunification and independence.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one
